uncited: It solves the performance bottleneck of software-based ray casting by utilizing 3D texture memory for trilinear interpolation and programmable shaders for front-to-back compositing [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

It differs from [Shear-Warp](shear-warp.md) by avoiding the final warp step and performing classification after resampling, and from [Custom Hardware Units](8284-custom-hardware-units.md) by relying on general-purpose programmable GPUs rather than dedicated ASICs [9529-3d-texture-mapping.md][8284-custom-hardware-units.md].
All methods in this family implement the emission-absorption optical model defined in [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md).
The core pipeline for each pixel consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and compositing [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

**Ray Generation**: Rays are generated per-pixel, typically by computing ray parameters from camera matrices in vertex/fragment shaders or by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry to determine entry/exit points [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
**Hardware-Accelerated Sampling**: Scalar volume values are sampled using the GPU's texture hardware.

The volume data is stored in 3D texture memory, and the texture engine performs trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels in parallel, avoiding manual shader interpolation [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
**Fragment Shader Compositing**: The ray marching loop, including classification and front-to-back compositing, is executed within the fragment shader [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
**Early Ray Termination (ERT)**: Rays are terminated when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) to optimize performance [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
It renders proxy geometry (coarsely tessellated bounding volume) to a fragment shader.
The vertex shader computes MCOP projection using equations 1 and 2, passing normalized and unnormalized projected coordinates to the fragment stage.

Hardware-assisted volume rendering emerged as a paradigm to overcome the computational limits of software-based ray casting.

Custom hardware units were developed earlier to address specific bottlenecks in geometry calculations and compositing for regular datasets, using fixed-function logic and DSPs [8284-custom-hardware-units.md].

The integration of programmable shaders allowed for more flexible implementations, such as the VStudio framework, which decouples rendering logic into modular components [6916-vstudio-framework-volume-rendering-pipeline.md].
More recent developments, such as Triton-accelerated raycasting, focus on optimizing memory bandwidth and kernel fusion for high-resolution rendering [3379-triton-accelerated-volume-raycasting.md].
